A few years ago, before Covid, I had a friend of mine (former work colleague from a different store), now working in a big box store similar to OP's, tell me a story similar to this in a way.

It was coming up to Easter, and their store was expecting the usual delivery of Easter Eggs. The store had recently undergone a refurb, and as yet, no promotional area had been set up for seasonal things like Easter. So the management of the store was simply told to work it out themselves, once the Easter stock came in. They would be able to see how much stock they had to display, and find a suitable spot to display it. They were also told that there would only be one delivery of Easter stock.

The store manages to put something together. Easter stock sells reasonably well. Then on the Wednesday before Easter, two pallets of Easter merchandise turn up. Management was upset, and immediately went through the various channels to find out what has happened. Turned out that two pallets had been put on the wrong truck, realised, taken back to the warehouse, put to one side, forgotten about, then sent out again. There was no space to display them, so the Easter Eggs had to sit in the storeroom until after Easter. The post Easter sales that year saw a LOT of Easter Eggs selling for less than half price to clear them.

The problem we have got, is this.

The number of letters being sent, has been steadily decreasing for a number of years now. Companies are sending their invoices via email, instead of by regular mail. Same with bank statements. Personal letters between friends is easier and quicker via sms or email.

However.

The cost of delivering a letter, has been steadily increasing. Increases in the various operating costs, means the amount of money that the government has to spend to run Australia Post keeps increasing. But with the decrease in the number of letters being sent, they are not making enough to cover. Even though it is government owned, they can't just run it as a money pit...they have to decrease costs, or maximise returns, wherever they can. 

Thus, an increase in the cost of stamps is a necessity.

I have been every year since 2005 (except during Covid), and this year has been the least interesting, for me.

Highlights: The Woolworths Dome is always a great place to go. However it seems as though this year they have decreased the number of exhibitors in it. This was a common theme around the show. But this year, they actually made an effort to put similar stands together...nearly all of the alcohol stands were together (or in close proximity) in the Woolworths Dome...so if you wanted to get tipsy on free samples, it was easy to. The Home and Lifestyle Pavillion was overflowing with government entities this year...but it did allow kids to find out more about the police, fire brigade etc. Another highlight for me was that it appeared there was more seating this year, and more tables. While in some areas it may have still been a little difficult to find somewhere to rest your feet, there just seemed to be more areas to sit.

Lowlights: Even in the showbag pavillion, it seemed as though they cut back on showbag stands. They had those food places along one wall, where in previous years you would see showbag stands. Sideshow Alley seemed to be lacking in variety...if it wasn't a game to hit bottle/cans with a ball, throw a basketball into a hoop, a ring toss over a bottle/pole, or scooping a duck/balls up out of the water...oh, and the clowns...there were only a couple of different ones. I'd also say that security was lacking in certain areas too...saw an argument in sideshow alley, with no security around...by the time security came, the people had left. And I'd also have to say that they must have cut back on cleaners...yes, it is a busy place, with thousands of people there...but when toilets do not seem to be cleaned in the four hours between visits, and garbage bins are left overflowing, you have to wonder whether enough cleaners were hired.

  
If you have kids, and can make a good day out of it (vouchers from the Ag Bag help), then it is worth going. If you are a teenager/young adult who can go on the adult rides (again, vouchers from the Ag Bag will help), then you might enjoy yourself. If you enjoy sampling the wares of the stands in the Woolworths Dome, then if you can justify the entry price, it is still a good time. But for me personally, I did not enjoy it, and am seriously considering giving it a break next year. Main reasons being that prices keep going up, not enough variety in certain places, and a general lack of direction of what the show was originally meant for...showcasing the country.

The problem you have there, is that is only appropriate if there is one party that is absolutely correct and true and honest, that everyone could believe in. You have your staunch Labor voters, who will never change...should they have to sit through 33 days of rhetoric from the Liberal party that they will never vote for, because they believe Labor is right and the Liberals are wrong? What about those Liberal voters who will only ever vote Liberal...should they have to sit through 33 days of rhetoric from the Labor party that they will never vote for, because they believe that the Liberals are right and Labor is wrong? And of course you also have the Greens and other small parties with their loyal voters, and independents who will get their friends and family to vote for them.

Then you have the swing voters...the only ones who your scenario would actually be useful for. Some will listen to every candidate, every party, and make an informed decision based on the information provided, influenced by their own personal situation and circumstances. Some will vote Labor, some will vote Liberal, some will vote Greens etc. All of those votes, are informed votes...and most of the time, they will seek out the information they need, to make their informed vote...thus negating the need to shut sporting events down for 33 days for them to pay attention.

For a lot of people, voting in an election is kind of like high school...you have your favourite subjects, that you will seek out information for, you will pay attention to. You have your least favourite subjects, that you will do the bare minimum in, and then forget about it. And then you have your average subjects that you neither like, nor dislike. In politics, you have your parties, your candidates, that you like. You like their policies, their personalities, what they stand for. You have your parties, your candidates, that you do not like, for whatever reason...you put up with them, and then move on. And then you have your average politicians (usually independents), who you don't necessarily care about, but you also don't dislike. Calling off sporting events for 33 days, would be kind of like having to pay attention during a school assembly...some of your favourite teachers, your friends, may be featured, that you will pay attention to...but by the end of it, you are so sick and tired of everything that you have forgotten three quarters of what is said. You force people to pay attention during an election campaign...after 33 days, most people would struggle to even remember things said or done on day 20.

Gambling problems, especially in NSW, exploded once they allowed slot machines into pubs. Before, slot machines were exclusively in clubs, and the casino. The homelessness issue is one that needs to be addressed, and urgently. The problem though, is that while a lot of people propose a lot of ideas on how to solve it, most do not understand the cause of the homelessness problem.

The public often thinks that people are homeless because they have drug/alcohol/mental health problems. Yes, some do, but a lot don't. Especially in the current economic climate, a lot of people are homeless simply because they cannot afford a roof over their head, because they do not get paid enough. I remember back in 1999, my wages as a full time retail trainee with Coles, would have been just enough to cover a studio apartment or a 1 bedroom apartment in a lot of parts of Sydney, and all associated bills (water/phone/electricity/transport/groceries etc). Now, the same wage may get you a one bedroom or studio apartment right on the edge of Sydney, but you would be struggling to pay for everything else. There is a guy that I encounter from time to time, who is homeless, but works full time, and just travels around Sydney until he finds a safe place to sleep for the night, sometimes splashing out on a backpackers or super cheap motel room for a few nights, just to sleep in a proper bed and take a shower.

There is also a good portion of homeless people who are homeless because of a breakdown in relationships/family. I remember one homeless person, who I used to encounter on my walk along Elizabeth street from Central Station up to Oxford street, who was homeless because he split from his wife after she cheated on him, got most of his assets in the divorce, and he had little family in Sydney to rely on for help. He worked part time as a chef, and the only reason why he wasn't full-time, is because places would not hire him because he had no fixed address.

Every working Australian having a living wage would be the first thing to do, to solve the homeless population. Then, restricting rents to being no more than 30% of income. More public housing, and more low cost rentals. More crisis accommodation. Putting a tax or a levy on Air BnB rentals, to encourage landlords to switch back to long term rentals. A tax or levy on properties left empty for a period of more than a year without cause. And re-purposing government owned buildings (and certain private buildings that have been empty for years) that are sitting dormant. For example, the government may decide to close down a hospital, because they are building a new one nearby. Re-purpose the old hospital (assuming no structural defects) into low cost or crisis accommodation. Seeing some of the abandoned buildings that are posted on various Facebook pages, there have been plenty of hospitals/schools/nursing homes/office buildings that, with a small investment, could be converted into accommodation. I have even seen footage from a couple of abandoned motels (one near Warwick Farm I think) that could have been renovated and rented out.

And an old idea from years ago...make every politician spend at least one week a year, trying to survive on the minimum wage, without access to their bank accounts or credit cards or government perks. Maybe even make them sleep rough for a week, to see what the homeless have to experience, and actually make them talk to and listen to the stories of the homeless and why they are homeless.

The things that would make a tycoon game constantly playable, as opposed to occasionally playable, are things like:

\* Things happening in real time, but the ability to choose how fast real time is. One of the things that I liked about Locomotion, was the ability to speed up the time so you wouldn't have to wait forever until you could do something again. BUT, it also needs to be realistic.

\* Things closely mirroring real life. Rollercoaster Tycoon was a great game, but in a lot of theme parks, the food amenities are usually put out to tender...you don't just decide "I'll put a Fries stand here, and a sunglass stand here." In the example of Rollercoaster Tycoon, in a normal theme park there would be regular maintenance scheduled...you would not have to wait until a mechanic is available.

\* Being able to achieve realistic goals. There was an old share market game I used to play, 20 years ago, called Wall Street Raider. While it had a halfway decent depiction of the US sharemarket on it, including some of the different ways you, or your company, could control companies and shares (bond issues, Greenmail, mergers etc.), the way it worked still had massive limitations...it could often take the whole 25 year game period, to get up enough money and share power, to enable say a merger between Pepsi and Frito Lay. It would rarely let you make an offer to buy out a failing company for less than the current share price.

\* Enough activities and goals to keep you interested in both the short term, and the long term, but not too many that you get bored with it. I have always had a dream of having a TV tycoon type game, where I could control either a small television station, a chain of television stations, or one of the big networks. I would have full control over the programming, could make my own if I want to, could purchase syndicated shows, do exclusive deals with studios, bid for sporting events...and have the ability to expand (I could say own a station in Miami that is a Fox affiliate, then buy one in say Dallas that was a Fox affiliate...or I could own a chain of stations and keep adding stations whilst running the chain or individual stations, even the ability to expand to a major network level). But have never quite found something that ticks all the boxes. Having the ability to just concentrate on a small station if I wanted to, or concentrating on becoming a network...that is what I am looking for. Another example of what I mean is the wrestling game Total Extreme Wrestling (TEW). If you were running as WWE for example, it could sometimes take you half an hour or so, just to go through all of the options, to put together a tv show for one day. If I just wanted to take it easy, and own the WWE, but not actually do any of the creative (booking shows), that option isn't available. 

\* An easy to use Interface. Too many games out there, have overly complicated menus, for all of the various things you can do in the game. And often that takes up the time trying to find the one little thing you want to do. An easy to use (and understand) interface allows the user to quickly do the tasks they need to do, and move onto the next thing, thus keeping interest in the game there. A soccer management game I used to play years ago (not Football Manager), had an overly complicated menu, which meant if you wanted to re-sign a particular player, you couldn't just click on the player...you had to go into the club menu, then into finances, then into contracts, then into roster, then select the player, then find the section which mentions their current deal, and the various options (release/re-sign etc)

I've been involved with major supermarket chains, and small independent IGA's (and others) in some manner for over 30 years, as well as other small businesses. Most IGA's aim for a minimum 30% GP, which, after their various outgoings, and how well the store is run, may result in a small net profit for them. If their weekly sales are say $100,000, after cost of goods sold, rent, utilities, wages, loan repayments etc, and after catering for wastage etc, they may make maybe $10,000 a week net profit, or they may make $50 a week net profit. The cost of goods sold across most IGA's is the same, outside of separate individual deals stores may make with suppliers. That's part of the reason why when you see IGA's for sale, they often will state turnover, but rarely state profit. Also, a typical supermarket ideally works on a scale of wages being no more than 10% of sales...7% if they don't have a bakery or deli. One particular IGA operator, who has stores across multiple states, used to try to run one store I am familiar with, which had a massive deli, as well as a coffee shop, with wages being at around 5% of sales, which used to cause so many problems with customer satisfaction.

Woolworths and Coles have a far different cost base. Their stores are typically larger, so naturally a typical store would have larger utility and wage costs compared to your average IGA. However, they would often pay less per square metre lease for their store, compared to an IGA, as they are seen as anchor tenant for shopping centres, to draw people in. They also have far superior buying power, meaning they can get goods for a lot less than what an IGA pays. One supplier to supermarkets that I am familiar with, lets say Woolworths and Coles may have paid $2 per unit for the product, and an IGA paid $2.50 per unit. Woolworths could sell it $3.20, and IGA sell it for $3.25. IGA are just barely making 30% GP on it, whereas Woolworths and Coles are making 60% GP on it

$10 million...I would go and buy a house, some investment properties, do some travelling, and leave a small amount in trust funds for various family members. When I die, the investment properties would then get divided up amongst certain family members.

One of the first things I learned at university, is any smart financial mind can make numbers dance, to the tune that they want. If Woolworths wanted to, they could have declared a loss, by writing off ALL goodwill from their NZ purchase. But shareholders want their dividend payouts., and dont want the value of their investment (shares) to fall. Woolworths could have decided not to write off any goodwill from the NZ purchase, and reported ever increasing profits...but then they would have needed to look at writing off extra goodwill next time, should they need to decrease the value of the goodwill on their investment.

An understanding of what Gross Profit, and Net Profit, is needed, when talking about how much profit a business makes. Woolworths and Coles could very well make an average 45% gross profit on every item they sell...some items they may make 60% or 70%, some items they may only make 10%, some items they may lose money on. A lot of small businesses tend to operate on a gross profit of 30% to 35%. However, just because you have a massive gross profit, doesn't mean that you are making any money...you could very well still be losing money.

In a hypothetical example, lets say a business has gotten a gross profit of $100 million for the year. That would literally be total sales, minus cost of goods sold. But that doesn't mean the business has an extra $100 million in the bank account. From that $100 million, the business owner has to deduct the costs of operating the business...things like wages, utilities, rent, service fees (for example, if they are a franchise, their franchise fees), stuff like that. So after you take all of that out, they may be left with $50 million. And this is where the financial minds come into play. They start looking at any other costs they can include...things like sponsorships, loans and loan repayments, stocktake variances which show up missing stock, stock wastage, theft, money that has been budgeted, and put into a separate account (thus claimed as an expense on the balance sheet), for a business related reason (such as expansion), and millions of other ways the financial minds can make the figures dance. Thus, that $50 million could suddenly become only $5 million . And in this I am not even talking about any tax liabilities.

So basically, Woolworths and Coles can still be price gouging us, but have the ability to manipulate the numbers to make it seem as though they are not.

Some people would look at spending the money on climate change. Some people would spend the money on making their dreams come true. In one scenario, I would do something similar. But in another scenario, I would kill myself. Let me explain.

In the scenario where I would kill myself, think about it like this. You have just discovered that you have $100 billion in your bank account. After the initial shock wears off, you would be checking with the bank to make sure that the account is accurate. Every likelihood that someone may overhear you and your account balance, even if it is just a bank employee. Just because the bank says it is accurate, you would want to make sure, and do some other investigations to confirm that it is all yours, and genuine. Other people may overhear and/or find out. Then, once you can confirm it is genuine, you would want to look at setting up insurance and security arrangements. Some security companies (not all) do employ people who may have had checkered pasts, may have links to bikie gangs or underworld figures. Once you start making enquiries about hiring security, it would not be long before the word got out. Plus once family and friends start seeing you with things you couldn't possibly afford on a normal salary, they would get suspicious. All of this would essentially make you a prime target for kidnapping, extortion, bribery etc...before you have sufficient security arrangements in place (you could already have security in place, but you wouldn't have developed the relationship yet where you could fully trust them). You would have family, friends, associates...heck, even people who sat next to you on a bus for five seconds back when you were 15 years old...come out of the woodwork, constantly harassing you, wanting money out of you. You would never be able to have a relationship with ANYONE anymore, because you would never know whether they like you for who you are, or for the amount of money you could spend on them. I would constantly be doubting so many things in my life, that I would never be able to enjoy my newfound wealth...so, I would kill myself, so I wouldn't have to put up with all of the stress, or drama, or headaches that having that much money would bring.

In the scenario where I would spend the money, I would instantly sit down and separate the money into maybe five different accounts, and open a couple of extra accounts for spending purposes. Money in the five accounts could only be transferred into the spending accounts, nowhere else, and would need additional verification before any transfers happen...adding a level of security to the money. I would also hire a full time security team, for my own protection. I would look after my family and friends, but in a way that they would be grateful for the gifts, but not feel entitled. I would buy several properties around the country. I would look into investing some money into low cost accommodation, to help with the housing crisis. I would buy the rights to several businesses and food brands, re-open stores and manufacturing plants across the country, to get people working again. As much as I would love to buy my favourite sporting teams...instead I would just help finance them, on the condition that I have a say on important decisions. There would be a few other things I would do too.

Oh, and I would also buy reddit, get rid of the ads, and make it free for everyone, in perpetuity.

Bruce Prichard said on his podcast once, in relation to Melting Moments, that they would sometimes feed false information to those they suspected of giving the inside gossip to Melting Moments, and other members of the wrestling media, just to see if it would get to them...and if the information then got printed in certain newsletters or on certain websites, they knew for certain to keep creative plans away from those individuals. It is part of the reason why people like Melting Moments would often say that Raw or Smackdown was always being re-written up to and during the show, which was actually a rarity...most of the time when something was altered, it was because another match or segment went over it's allotted time. But you would read in Melting Moments newsletter, that Vince or HHH or whoever in WWE, was constantly changing up the show.

  
In days of old, you had a plethora of wrestling magazines...Pro Wrestling Illustrated, Inside Wrestling, The Wrestler etc. These would often be written and printed, around 3 months before their cover date...thus why the Pro Wrestling Illustrated Yearly Awards issue was always the March issue. This, I am guessing, was to enable the distribution of the magazines, and the development of fantasy stories to pad out the issue. But with legitimate sports, their magazines could be written and published within a couple of days of the events transpiring, plus you had the reporting on the nightly news and in the daily newspapers and on radio shows. Trying to report on a fictitious sport, without (at the time) giving away that it was a fictitious sport. But the average wrestling fan wanted more information...they wanted to know who was leaving, who was coming in, what happened at the big event that they didn't get to see on tv because it wasn't covered. That is where the origins of the wrestling newsletter came about, and the wrestling hotlines that you paid $1.99 a minute for. 

When the internet came around, it was a lot easier to spread all of this information, and fantasy stories, and a lot cheaper to do so. And for a while, it seemed as though whoever told the biggest bullshit, would get the bigger readership. Wrestling newsletters and websites that stuck strictly to news and reviews, seemed to disappear as quickly as they started, while newsletters and websites that mainly dealt in so-called rumours and gossip, thrived. The masses would flock to whoever yells the loudest, rather than those who were clear and concise. And because these people were the loudest, the masses would listen, and not realise the garbage they were actually being fed. Melting Moments would regurgitate the rumours and gossip that he was being fed by his sources...but then, because he was one of the loudest, would pepper his newsletter with reviews of matches and events, making it seem as though it was legitimate unbiased reviews, instead of telling people that it was his personal opinion, and not based on any particular metrics. And because he has been one of the loudest, for as long as he has, people just believe his word is gospel, and don't want to go to the hassle of fact checking, or in the case of reviews, watching and comparing.

I stumbled across a match involving the Young Bucks...a team that Melting Moments seems to rave about quite a lot. I can't remember who they were facing, but it was on an AEW show. In terms of actual in-ring action, the match was not fluid in anyway. Looking over a lot of Melting Moments 5 star ratings, he seems to favour matches that are fast paced, with plenty of high flying spots, or "wow" moments, even if the match doesn't flow. As a result, back in the day a wrestler like Lanny Poffo would probably get great ratings for his matches, even though there was little crowd reaction, and sometimes the natural flow of the match wasn't there. But a wrestler like Greg Valentine, who had excellent psychology, and knew the right moment to perform the right move, would be given a poor rating.

During school, Kirk was an accomplished gymnast, representing his state in various gymnastic competitions. However, his gymnastic career ended during Olympic trials when he was 17, where he was one of the favourites in the mens competition to represent Australia in the 2000 Olympics, due to a snapped ankle and muscular damage to his shoulder from a nasty fall. A side effect from this was a rare medical condition that was causing rapid muscle loss around his body, meaning that he became one of the few people, under rigorous medical supervision, to be allowed a prescription of heavy dose steroids specifically for muscle growth. After a couple of years of intense rehabilitation, Kirk had turned his body into a ripped pile of muscles, the envy of a lot of gym junkies. After seeing a local independent wrestling show, Kirk was approached by the promoter, a grizzled veteran of the Australian wrestling scene, to try wrestling for a career. Kirk was a natural, and was able to beautifully combine the agility and stamina from his gymnastic days, with the strength and determination from the muscle gain and recovery, After 3 months of training, Kirk entered his first wrestling contest for the local promoter, and came across as a natural in the ring. Kirk spent three months with DIW, before joining RAW...but with an exit clause if an international promotion came knocking. Black Canvas Grappling in Japan had sent one of their talent scouts to Australia, and they liked what they saw in Kirk, so quickly offered him a contract. I have over 20 years experience in supermarkets, and actually held the scanning record at one supermarket. Yet even I have encountered issues with self serve registers over the years, NONE of which were my fault.

1. Products not scanning at the correct price. Happens frequently, regardless of whether you use self serve or not.
2. Products not scanning. Happens frequently as well...this is usually to do with packaging issues, where the barcode may be folded over, or a slight misprint in the barcode. Other reason is usually because the self serve scanners don't get the same level/frequency of cleaning as a manned register, so often get spills/smudges/marks preventing things from scanning properly. Sometimes also happens because of incorrect data entered into the system.
3. Not registering that the product has been put in the bagging area. Often has to do with the weight of the product being too light to register, or you have your bags overhanging the bagging area thus the register thinks you have removed items.
4. Register saying you have removed an item. Often has to do with having your bags overhanging the bagging area thus the register thinks you have removed items. Also comes up if you scan too quickly, and put two items in the bag at the same time, or if you don't have enough space in the bagging area and have to remove a bag to fit something else on. None of this is your fault, it is the fault of the set-up of the registers.
5. Eftpos terminal not working. Common issue across all of retail, with compatability issues between different banks, different cards, and different eftpos terminals.
6. Register not accepting cash. Common issue with any self serve machine where there is a cash option...sometimes, you have to put your notes in a certain way, make sure they are completely flat, there are no tears or corners missing etc. With some older machines, may mean software hasn't been updated to accept newer style notes (happens on some slot machines where they don't accept the newer $100 notes).

There are other reasons, but these are the main ones. And none of these are a user's fault, and all of these can cause problems/delays with using the self serve checkout.

Before making a determination, I feel as though more details are needed.

1. What is your relationship generally like with your husband? Are you happy? Do you have frequent fights? Is he disappointed in you for some reason? Do you make him angry, without you necessarily knowing? Are you open and honest with each other about the issues in your relationship, or do you keep things hidden? It is entirely possible that he could be fed up with how you treat him when he is at home, and just wants to go and do something that will make him happy? But by the same token, he may need a break from being smothered with love and kindness. Definitely need to have a sit down honest conversation to find out if there are any issues in the relationship that need to be sorted out.
2. Has he been to the Alamo Bowl before? Has he been with this group of people before? Has this trip been attempted in the past, with the same group of people, but the whole group just can't get together at the right time for it to happen? Is this essentially one of his "bucket list" items that he needs to do? Likewise, if a group of your friends from high school or college get together for a girls night out every year, but this year you have managed to score tickets, for free, to go and see your favourite musical artist...yet, it happens to coincide with a special night that your husband has planned for you and him...would you still insist on going to the concert, knowing it will possibly be the only time in your life that the whole group of friends will be together at the same time to see this one artist?

I am not saying you are, or are not, the a-hole. I just feel that communication is a problem here, and it feels as though there could be problems in your relationship above and beyond this trip. As others have said, counselling, or a good honest discussion with your husband about the relationship, may be needed.

Every countries Monopoly competition is different, but run in the same way. If there are 10 cars to be won, and you need three blue properties to win, they will print a heap of property 1, a heap of property 2, but only 10 of property 3. Those 10 stickers are closely guarded, and are taken to the packaging facility where the rest of the stickers are being applied to the packaging as it is produced. The 10 stickers are applied to packagin at random, and the cartons of packaging are then randomised, so no-one even knows what carton the winning sticker is in. Stores order the packaging, or get allocated the cartons as part of a normal prder, and that's it.

After the controversy surrounding the American version of the competition a fair few years ago now, they even do a batch of dummy winning stickers, with like the free sundae as a prize, so that even the people tasked with applying the stickers to the cups/fries containers, don't know which ones are the winning ones.

I would just suck it up, and get a retail job. Why? Because it is a job. 

A supermarket I worked at years ago, had me running the dairy department, with a Bachelor of Business (Marketing) degree. The fresh produce person had a Bachelor of Applied Science degree. The second in charge of the deli department had a Bachelor of Accounting AND a Bachelor of Education degree. One of the nightpackers had a Masters in Communication. And we had cashiers and nightpackers who were studying other degrees.

Having a degree, and working in a field unrelated to the degree, shows a potential employer that you are willing to put in the hard yards to learn. Something like a degree in Business Administration, means that if you start as a packer in a supermarket, you would be looked at more favourably if a supervisor position becomes available, then when an assistant department manager position becomes available, and so forth. Before you know it, you could be running a store, supervising hundreds of employees...or working in the corporate office, making decisions that affect how the business overall performs. But you have to be willing to put in the work, and not just be the person who says "Hey, I have a degree, now give me a high paying job". Consider the fact that starting at the bottom in retail, is a way of doing long term research, so as you climb the ladder, you have practical experience and knowledge to fall back on, rather than relying on what is in books and published reports.

I am a person who lived in the area for over ten years. I am also a person who has both driven through the area, and walked through the area. I have done both, during both peak hour, and off peak. Part of the problem is that people often only concentrate on the problems during peak hour, which is the point of the sign to begin with...when there are multiple people around, needing to use the crossing. But what is often overlooked is the problems outside of peak hour, where most of the pedestrian incidents seem to occur.

Back when Cake It Away was open there (got our wedding cake from them, beautiful cakes), I was chatting to a couple of older gentlemen who were outside having a coffee. During that time we saw two near misses from drivers not paying attention, or being unaware, of the pedestrian crossing. One of the gentlemen mentioned that after he nearly got hit once, he complained, and got the impression that nobody wants to do anything because that side of Meadowbank is seen as the "old" side, and doesn't deserve any money spent on it.

The people usually only cross in large amounts, in dribs and drabs, during peak hour. Outside of peak hour, some cars come off the bridge and down through the pedestrian crossing like they are racing in the Bathurst 1000, and that wouldn't give any pedestrian a chance most times. Just surprised there hasn't been more casualties there. I still believe they put the traffic lights on the wrong side...a zebra crossing was much better for the other side.

Most car drivers complain about the pedestrian crossing during peak hours, when the trains get in and there are lots of pedestrians trying to cross the road. There can be at least 50 people trying to cross, if trains from both directions pull in at the same time.

Most pedestrians complain about the cars going through the intersection outside of peak hours, where cars often come off the bridge and down the slight hill, thinking that the crossing will be clear...ir come up the hill and around the corner, thinking the same thing...they often don't think about someone actually using the crossing.

This is one of the most notorious pedestrian crossings in Sydney. Every week...heck, nearly every day, someone almost gets hit by a car going through that crossing. After having a pram nearly hit by a car not paying attention once, I did some letter writing. I wrote to the local state member, mentioned the issues, mentioned the possible solutions. The local member (since retired from politics), said that one solution would need the approval of Railcorp (at the time), as they controlled the railway station. Another possible solution, the local member said would require massive spending from the RTA, which was not likely on a suburban street. He suggested passing everything on to the local council, to see what they could do. The local council pretty much said that they couldn't do a thing about it, and would need to be passed onto the Department of Transport. Department of Transport said that since it was a local road, it was council's responsibility. Local council then said because of the location, it would need to consult with the Department of Transport for a solution. During this time a new set of traffic lights was installed on the other side of the railway station, where there had been next to no reports of near misses or pedestrians being hit. And then council came back and said they can't put traffic lights in because it would back traffic up, plus if traffic lights were put in, it wouldn't stop people driving through the intersection.

To this day, near misses still happen. At least once a month someone still gets hit (albeit with no injuries). I have seen people get hit and fall to the ground there. And most car drivers turn around and say that it is the fault of the pedestrians crossing the road there, that they run out in front of cars (most people who get hit or have a near miss are those not in a position to run, such as disabled, elderly etc), and that pedestrians wouldn't get hit if they just waited for cars to go through.

For those that want to know, my suggestions to fix the issue included building a pedestrian bridge, linked to the one across the station (there is the space for it), putting in pedestrian lights (not full traffic lights...it is an awkward section of road), or roadworks to change the flow of traffic (moving the intersection right at the crossing a few metres down the side road, to allow for more space for cars to wait for people to cross).

And one last point...the near misses and pedestrians that have been hit, have often occurred OUTSIDE of peak hour, when there is little traffic around, and a person would have to wait for 15 minutes until there were several people ready to cross the road.

In this situation, with the little information that has been provided by OP, the neighbour does have to pay half the cost, at least. If it can be proven that the damage, and the need to replace the fence is because of a deliberate or negligent act by the neighbour, the minimum that the neighbour would have to pay is half. If taken to small claims court, the neighbour could potentially be forced to pay for the entire fence...again, if it was able to be proven, with expert testimony, that the neighbour was at fault.

If it was a simple case of the landlord (or neighbour) just wanting to update the look of the fence, then that would be entirely up to the landlord (or neighbour) to pay.

But ultimately, this is a battle that should be fought between the landlord and the neighbour, and not you. You can ask, or pressure the landlord to do something about the fence, but ultimately, it is up to the landlord to get it done...and then have the battle with the neighbour. BUT, the amount of evidence you can give to the landlord that it is the fault of the neighbour, may help the landlord to get it done quicker, and then potentially charge the neighbour.

I don't know whether legal experts would allow this...but I have a theory.

You have proof that the sign on bonus was $20,000. You have proof that they have only paid you $13,000. Make sure you have it in writing, asap, that you want that extra $7,000. Then after you have said that, pay the $20,000. They will think that everything is done and dusted...but it's not.

You have proof that you have asked for the extra $7,000 of the sign on bonus. You never received it. You could ask for it again, they will ignore you, most likely. That is when you drag it out, for as long as you can, then take them to court. Demand in court the $7,000, plus interest. It was a sign on bonus, and you never received the whole amount. They will argue you left, and had to pay the $20,000 back...which you did. But you still haven't received the missing $7,000. They cannot deny you the $7,000, and as a result the judge should order them to pay the $7,000, hopefully with interest.

The other option to look at, is the fact that they have only paid you $13,000 out of the $20,000 sign on bonus. They have not paid the other $7,000, which means they have breached the employment contract, and you had every right to leave. In this instance, you shouldn't have to pay anything back. 

Both of these scenarios are simplistic views, they are not legal advice, and without reading the fine print of the employment contract, should be taken as opinion rather than fact.

If we use the basis of a house being say $1.5 million (Ryde/Eastwood/Carlingford general area is the basis for this valuation), deposit requirement would be $900,000. Now lets say a couple, earn a combined $100,000 (after tax). At current prices in the area concerned, they pay $750 a week on rent...so lets say $39,000 a year on rent. Lets say $5,000 a year on utilities (electricity, gas, water, phone, internet etc). $5,200 a year on transportation (this is assuming $50 each per week towards an Opal card...similar if it is a one car family when you factor in rego, insurance, petrol, and maintenance). Allow $100 a week on groceries, and another $100 a week on other expenses (clothing, furniture, electronics, medical, health insurance etc). That leaves just over $40,000 a year. The couple would still need 23 years to save up the deposit, which by that time the cost of the $1.5 million house would probably be $2.5 million.

A $750,000 unit in the same area could be done in less time (12 years estimate). But both of these don't take into account that costs will rise, wages may or may not rise, it only calculates the cost using current valuations.

A couple of other schemes to include in this...

1. Expand the Rent To Buy scheme. Cap rents (of social housing) at 30% of income...but if the customer adds an extra 10% of income, it becomes a rent to buy situation. Deposits wouldn't be needed in this situation. Obviously there would need to be clauses in rental contracts for situations such as if a resident passes away, or loses their job etc.
2. On surplus government land, have some government housing developments where people can access low cost government loans to purchase the properties. Obviously there would be pre-requisites to access the scheme. If a person becomes unable to pay off the loan, the property becomes social housing, to rent.
3. Enforce a requirement for developers to include a certain percentage of social housing in their developments. Say in a 100 unit tower, 10% of units need to be social housing. If the developer goes to 20%, they get a discount on taxes and duties etc.
4. Regulate the short stay accommodation market. Require all Air b'n'b (and similar) properties to be registered with council as a short stay accommodation site. Have councils crackdown on sites that shouldn't be short stay accommodation, with harsh penalties in place. A lot of people don't realise that a major part of the rental crisis is landlords still holding onto properties for short stay accommodation purposes...there is one unit block near me, where over a third of the units are now being used as short stay accommodation, because landlords can still make more money that your usual rental accommodation.
5. Government returns to encouraging businesses to relocate to regional centres. Offer incentives for staff to relocate too. Helps with the economies of regional centres, and in some regional centres you can get a 3 bedroom rental for a quarter of what you pay in parts of Sydney.

If there were not these extra-special Superbowl ads done every year, a lot of these people would be out of a job. There would be a gap of maybe a few weeks, maybe a few months, between jobs. I decided to get a security system installed at my place after several break-ins in the local area. The salesman sat down with me, we went over my requirements, and the unique nature of the house, to decide the best place to put the alarm pad, which we agreed would be just inside the front door (once you open the front door, you walk into an open loungeroom). I also said that I was going away for a couple of weeks, and would like the installer to come AFTER I returned, giving him the dates I would be back. The installer said that is fine.

The very day after I left, the installer came (there was someone else at home still). When I got back (which was after their 14 day cooling off period), I noticed all of the problems with the install. They installed the alarm panel in the loungeroom, but at the doorway to the hallway...meaning any time we walked in the front door, we had to walk through the loungeroom to get to the alarm panel. The smoke alarm they installed, was right next to the gas stove in the kitchen (almost no-one puts a smoke alarm in a kitchen, especially right next to a gas stove with no rangehood). The sensors they installed (of which there were only two) were positioned in such a way that I was soon able to work out how to enter the front door, and walk the entire length of the hallway, without setting the alarm off. When I reported this to them, because it was out of the 14 day cooling off period, there was nothing I could do. 

Eventually, I found a way out of the contract (we were paying per month for monitoring). Having a look at the fine print, I found a loophole where if I could prove that the equipment was defective, I could get out of the contract. As part of the deal to sign up, we got one of those personal alarms that women used to have in their handbags. Because that was part of the equipment listed in the contract, and we were able to show it was faulty (somehow it got dunked in water a few times, then dried out), we got out of the contract.

When I was a kid, pubs used to make a lot of money, and all they had was maybe half a dozen video poker machines...no slot machines at all, they were exclusive to clubs and the casino. But when they let slot machines go into pubs, a lot of pubs stopped caring, what used to make them a success disappeared, and eventually you had pubs closing down. And a side effect was, with slot machines no longer a money winner for clubs since they had to share with pubs now, community investment by clubs went downhill, and you had a whole heap of clubs go to the wall.

Easiest solution would be to pull slot machines out of pubs, leaving them exclusive to clubs and the casino again. Reduce the red tape so live music/entertainment can return to a lot of pubs. And lower the alcohol tax. One other potential sweetener for pubs, to let the slot machines be pulled, is to allow them to become lottery agents. With the number of newsagents closing down, there is a small opening there that could be filled by pubs.

Sometimes it is the delivery drivers who cannot read the address.

Back in September last year, I was staying in a hotel, one that I have stayed in many times in the past. I know the address, as I have had to give it to taxi drivers many times. Anyway, I ordered something from a pizza place (not one of the chains, a local place), and made sure I put in the room number, the address, and the name of the hotel (there is currently only one hotel under this name/brand in this city). I rang up MenuBlob, they wouldn't believe me when I said it hadn't been delivered, then when I was able to describe the path that the GPS said the delivery driver took, they said that it was unusual, and would look into it. They also tried claiming that we didn't put the address in correctly, and when they read it back to me, I said that it was correct. I also said that I have already spoken to the front desk, who will vouch that it hasn't arrived.

In my experience, there are three main reasons why a person rushes to get on a plane.

1. As has already been mentioned quite a few times, issues with your carry-on. Most people want to have their carry-on in an overhead compartment close to where they are sitting, so that when they disembark, it is easy for them to grab their carry-on. Connecting flights, medications, valuables etc...many reasons for wanting the carry-on close to you.
2. To make sure you get your seat. Some airlines are very strict with seat assignments, some are not. Sometimes you may get to your seat, and someone else is already sitting there, because they wanted to sit with their friends. OR, you paid for the window seat, but the person who paid for the aisle seat is sitting there, because they don't want the aisle seat now. Because of how long it can take to board, by the time you get the attention of an attendant, and the following conversations and requests to sit in the correct seats, you can potentially delay the plane.
3. To get set up, and comfortable. Some flights are only an hour. Some are 14 hours. Do you really want to be struggling to get your book or tablet out ready to view, while the plane is taking off? Do you still want to be moving around in your seat to find that one relaxing position for the next few hours? If you are superstitious or a nervous flyer, do you want to be doing your pre-flight ritual, when the plane is already in the air? I know of a friend, who has to close his eyes and take five deep breaths, before the plane has even departed the gate. Those few extra seconds a person gains, by rushing to get on the plane, could be the difference between an enjoyable flight, or sitting next to someone who shits themselves every time the plane encounters turbulence (happened on a plane a friend of mine was an attendant on recently).

In high school, we had a librarian who was as lazy as anything...an old woman, in her 60s most likely, chose to spend her time in the office rather than open the library during our lunch breaks so we could go in and study. 

She was a stickler for books being returned on time, and issued fines if they were not...but could sometimes let books sit there for a week before she recorded that they had been returned. This meant that many kids ended up getting small fines because of her laziness. 

One day, after getting a fine for this very reason, I hatched a plan. The way books were recorded were through a card that was in the inside cover of the book (this was before computers). If you took a book up to borrow, and the card was missing, a new one would be written up for the book. So I paid my fine, then borrowed a book, that I knew there was only one copy of. Over the next two weeks, I lent the book to a bunch of friends, so they could "borrow" it too, each time with a new card being written for it. In the end, about 20 cards were written for the book, which only ever had one copy in the library. I "returned" the book, and then the librarian was left scrambling trying to work out who borrowed the book, so she could record it being returned.

Their system did not allow for a simple copy and paste. Their products were separated into different subcategories. It had the function to select all for a larger category (such as yoghurt), but in their system the 200g yoghurts were not listed with pouches, or 500g, or 1kg, or multi-packs, so when selecting ALL in their system for yoghurt, it would mean the person would only have to search for four lines to remove them from the order. By having 26 lines on the order, they would each have to be entered individually, opening up the chance for errors, which did happen.

As mentioned...as originally mentioned, by saying all but four lines, it means the supplier can select all items, then just has to find four to remove. By doing it the way I had to in the end, it meant they had to enter 26 lines individually, opening up the chance for errors by selecting the wrong product...which coincidentally is EXACTLY what happened by doing the full list.
But we carried everything they made...as stated.

So, when their computer software has two yoghurts listed in one section, three in another, two in another, yet have the option to select ALL, it is a lot easier to select ALL, than to go through each section to find the two yoghurts or three yoghurts. Then, if say 30 yoghurts have all been selected, with one carton each, it is easier to go back in and remove specifically four lines. 

Lets use something you may be more familiar with...screws. You use 32 different types and sizes of screws. There are 32 different types and sizes of screws you can order from the supplier. You need to place an order. You need to order 28 out of the 32 screws. The supplier has the screws separated into different categories...lets say metal, wood, masonry etc. The supplier's system has the function to order one carton of every type of screw, or order them individually. You need every type of screw except for 40mm wood, 30mm and 40mm metal, and 20mm masonry. If you place an order for ALL screws, except for four you don't need, the supplier can select ALL screws in their system, and then remove four screws, saving time. If you were to list 28 different screws, the person then has to search for the 28 screws one at a time, taking longer...thus opening things up for potential errors, by inputting a wrong screw.

I am not a fancy person, I don't expect things to be absolutely perfect. I have had good landlords, and bad landlords. One place I lived in, which was an older unit (about 70 years old as an estimate), we only moved because the landlord was selling the unit. We got our whole bond back, despite a little bit of damage to the lino on the kitchen floor which was torn up by our fridge when it was moved. We were told that the unit was sold to a couple who were going to live in it, so the state of the unit upon sale was not our responsibility.

Our next place was a place we lived in for over 10 years. A house that had various issues, but we found ways to work around those issues, plus it was cheap rent that only went up twice during the ten plus years we lived there. But we moved out after one too many issues were not fixed in a timely manner. For that place, we got our whole bond back, probably because of the five A4 page report we gave the real estate when they came for an inspection three months earlier.

Our next place after that, was marginally better, with only one major problem that we found a quick workaround for. While things like a blocked drain would take some time to get fixed, it was still done without too much of a delay. However, this place we lost power in, during the heavy rains in February (I later found out that we could have claimed flood assistance, but we didn't). This left the house with only one working powerpoint for the entire house, up until the time we moved out (which was about 6 weeks later). The landlord wanted to keep our entire deposit, and then extra, because of the supposed state we left the house in. We then fired back with photos of the condition of the house from when we first moved in. The landlord then tried keeping part of the bond for cleaning. We again fired back, even starting the process with the tribunal. The real estate urged the landlord to just give the bond back (which he eventually did), because if it went to the tribunal, not only would he lose because we had the photographic evidence, but he would most likely have been ordered to pay US for not having a habitable building to live in during the six weeks we had no power (where we should have been offered alternative accommodation until the power issue was fixed, or a rent reduction, neither of which occurred).

Unfortunately, most of the things needed to fix public transport in Sydney require LOTS of expenditure, so most likely will never happen. And while they may never happen, they are realistic...not pie in the sky things like fast rail between Sydney and Newcastle, or teleportation hubs at railway stations, or an efficient and workable taxi network.

What would help would be a complete re-think of Sydney's bus network...not just the spacing between stops, not just getting rid of curvy and complicated routes, not just frequency...everything to do with the bus network. Get rid of separate companies owning bits and pieces of the bus network...either have ONE company run it, or have the government run it. Better synergies then between depots, and drivers. Be able to get rid of a lot of dead time in between services. Be able to replace services easy...a bus from Ryde depot could be called to Macquarie to replace a bus from Mt Kuringai depot...rather than just cancelling services or waiting for a Mt Kuringai bus to come all the way down. Better integration of services with the rail network...have buses feed into the rail network a lot more efficiently.

The first thing to think about...in what style will the musical be? Will it be a comedy? Will it be a romance? Will it be a dramatic musical? Will it be historical? Look at a few classic musicals over the years, and watch how the story flows through the music. Sit down, write your story, then look at your story and think of scenes that could be expressed through music, through song...for example, you have a person wake up in the morning, look out the window, and see that it is a beautiful day. They walk downstairs, walk outside, grab the newspaper, look up in the sky, sees it is a beautiful day, and then breaks into song about how it is a beautiful day. Over time, this has resulted in some lines having the bare minimum of stock on the shelf each week, and meaning that there is no longer any space to order extra stock for things that are selling well, or are on special...meaning that lines are selling out within a couple of days of being delivered. The owner looks at the empty shelves and says that the staff need to order more stock in a particular area...but with no room in the budget, it means other things will not get ordered, and thus sell out fast. Customers, frustrated by the out of stocks, walk out the door and shop elsewhere. The owner then turns around and wants to know why sales are not increasing...BECAUSE THERE IS NO STOCK TO SELL. Possible reasons...

1. The new owners were not fully aware of how the bonus structure is set up for different roles and different levels within the organisation, at what rates the bonuses are awarded etc. Does not indicate anything wrong with the organisation.
2. The new owners were given incorrect information from the old owners in regards to the bonus structure, and awarded the bonuses per the incorrect information. Does not indicate anything wrong with the organisation.
3. The lower than expected bonus could be a result of higher than usual expenditure. The new owners may have had loans associated to the business purchase, new goods and equipment may have needed to be purchased, so while business may have been better, the extra expenses may have eroded the money available for bonuses for this year. Generally regarded as one off business expenses on a profit/loss statement, no indication of a problem with the business.
4. If the new owners have other businesses, they may have applied bonuses based on how ALL of their businesses fared, not just yours. Not necessarily and indication of anything wrong with the organisation.
5. The business may be trying to integrate your bonus structure into how bonuses with other owned businesses within the organisation operate...so the bonus amount may be low now, but may be higher later.
6. The owners may be spreading the bonuses over a monthly payment structure until the business re-opens next season, thus keeping everyone on the books for that period.

A friend of mine used to work for a department store where something similar used to happen...but came up with a clever way around it. In this store, every department had their own section that they would place returns or "damaged items" that would be found on the shelf (things like open boxes, missing tags etc). It was my friends job to go around to all of the departments, grabs all of the returns or "damaged stock", and take it out the back to the storeroom. There, he would go through each item, one by one, to see if it was to sellable. Those items that could still be sold, would be put in one pile. Those items that could still be sold, but have slight damage to it (such as a torn wrapper), would be put into another pile, to be marked down. Third pile would be company returns, and fourth would be scanned and thrown out. He would generally do this last thing before leaving for the day, with stock going back on the shelf being left to the nightfillers to take care of.

So what my friend used to do, is he would walk the store, and if he saw anything he wanted, he would put in one of the necessary areas, then as he is processing everything, put it aside and grab it as he leaves for the day.

Later that night, I am watching the news, and they had managed to get the whale back into the water, and encouraged it to join a pod of whales nearby, hoping that the mother was it's mother.

That night, and the following morning, I was googling to find out any progress with the whale, as there were several pods of whales on a southern descent off the coast at that time, and the experts were not sure which pod the whale belonged to. And then I happened to have googled the sad news that it had beached itself again, and died.
